title: Who Are You

post.author: u/quillhaven_gate_mihnea
post.title: I guard a gated estate at night. At 02:14 the barrier opened for Mrs Haverkamp's account, from a phone it had never seen. She is abroad until the 26th.

blocks.text: I'm Mihnea, night guard at Quillhaven: 410 houses behind one barrier, and my hut beside it. Residents open the barrier from a phone app, and my screen lists every opening with the house number.

First the app must prove who is asking. Proving who someone is is called authentication. A phone signs in once with the resident's password; then the app keeps a session, its record that this phone is that resident's (as in The Letter With No Return Address). A new phone must give the password.

The app doesn't store passwords as typed. A fixed recipe turns each one into a jumble that can't be turned back, the way a fingerprint can't become a finger. The same password always gives the same jumble. That jumble is a hash; at sign-in the app hashes what you type and compares.
Portcullis, the firm that built our app, used a fast hash: checking one guessed password against a jumble costs almost nothing, for the app and for anyone holding a copy.

It also added nothing to each password first. That something would be a few random letters, different for every resident, kept beside the jumble: a salt. Without one, the same password gives the same jumble, so one guess checks every account at once.
All of it lives in the app's database, its store of accounts. On 3 August someone at Portcullis saved a copy of it, called a backup, with every jumble inside.

It was left on a public file share, a web folder anyone with its address can open. At 16:20 yesterday a stranger emailed our residents' association about it. Our chair, Mr Nkemdirim, read it at 07:30 today.

Mrs Haverkamp moved into 14 Hawthorn Walk on 22 July. On 5 October she left a note at my hut: away until the 26th, please watch the house. Here is her account's gate log: date and time, which phone asked (phone 1 is hers), and what the barrier did.

22 Jul  16:05  phone 1  opened, first sign-in
04 Oct  18:40  phone 1  opened
05 Oct  05:52  phone 1  opened
15 Oct  02:14  phone 2  opened, first sign-in

blocks.label: barrier_night_14_oct.png

diagram.aria: The night from 21:00 on 14 October to 04:00 on 15 October. Two phones the app had never seen signed in. At 21:52 the man at 3 Damson Row, with his own new phone; the barrier opened. 14 Hawthorn Walk shows nothing from 21:00, its owner away since 5 October, until 02:14, when phone 2 signed in with her password and the barrier opened.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from my screen's list. Two first sign-ins all night: at 21:52 the man at 3 Damson Row, whose car I know, on a phone he bought that day; at 02:14 phone 2, on Mrs Haverkamp's account. Both gave the right password, and the barrier opened both times.

blocks.text: At 02:14 the camera showed a grey car I didn't know. By the time I walked to number 14, it had gone. Her door was locked.

At noon the association's security adviser, Dilnoza Yusupova, reported on the copy. A slow hash, she wrote, makes every check costly on purpose, with a cost setting that can be raised. With a salt too, every guess is separate work for every account.

Her numbers: 1,240 accounts. 312 use a password from a published list of the most common ones; 41 more use one from another website's leak. Stored as ours were, treat 893 as exposed, known to whoever has the copy: those 353 and 540 more. Stored slow and salted, the 353 would still be exposed; the other 887 would hold. Mrs Haverkamp's is on the common list, and in that other leak.
The barrier opened for the right password. Every line of the log is true.
Portcullis wants to change something tonight, and Mr Nkemdirim wants an email out to every resident. Before they start: what should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your adviser's two numbers are the interesting ones: 893 and 353. Storage decides how many passwords a stolen copy gives away. It can do little for a password that is common, or that already sits in another website's leak. Using one password on several sites is called password reuse. Now look at the phone column of your log. What did the app know about phone 2 at 02:14?

replies.author: u/quillhaven_gate_mihnea
replies.text: That it was a first sign-in, the same as 21:52. Dilnoza's report adds that 34 of the 1,240 accounts have no phone number on file at all; they joined before the app asked for one. 24 of those 34 are among the 893.

comments.author: u/new_password_pemberton
comments.text: Every few months my bank makes me pick a new password. Forcing a new password every few months is what the banks do, and banks know security. Do it every 90 days at Quillhaven and any leaked password is dead within a season. Simple, cheap, no new gadgets for anyone to lose.

comments.author: u/portcullis_dev_wojtek
comments.text: Wojtek from Portcullis. The backup was mine, and I'm sorry. Tonight I can move every password to a slow hash with its own salt: Argon2id, the one that OWASP, a volunteer project that publishes security guidance, names first. Each password moves the next time its resident signs in, because that's when the app sees it typed. The next copy that leaks would give away 353, not 893.

comments.author: u/quillhaven_chair_nkemdirim
comments.text: Chair here. Only the share's owner at Portcullis can delete the file, and she lands at 18:00. The minute she does, it goes, and every resident gets an email saying so. A file nobody can reach can't hurt anybody.

reply.prompt: Portcullis wants to change something tonight. What should Quillhaven change before the next copy, or the next stranger at 02:14? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Make residents change their passwords every 90 days, so a leaked one stops working quickly.
options.part2: The association voted for a new password every 90 days, starting in November, and the app now nags each resident on day 90. In the sim I turned the rule on and replayed the night. Mrs Haverkamp set her password on 22 July, 85 days before 02:14, so no change was due until 20 October: phone 2 opened the barrier at 02:14 exactly as before. The copy still showed 893 of 1,240 accounts exposed; a calendar doesn't change how a copy was stored. In December the first round came due, and at the barrier I heard two residents compare notes: each had kept the old password and changed the number on the end. Pemberton's bank rule gave us more passwords, not better ones.
options.senior: Forced periodic changes look like a timer on leaks, but a leaked password can be used the same night, and people on a schedule usually make a small, guessable change to the old one. NIST SP 800-63B says verifiers SHALL NOT require periodic changes, and SHALL force a change when there is evidence of compromise, as there is now for the 893. Check every new password against a list of common and leaked ones, and ask for a second proof when a new phone signs in. A rule about when passwords expire leaves how they are stored, and whether a stranger can use one, untouched.

options.text: Ask for a code from the resident's own phone whenever a new phone tries to open the gate.
options.part2: Portcullis added it in a week: when a phone the app has never seen signs in, the barrier waits for a code sent by text message to the phone number on file, and opens only when that code is typed into the app. In the sim I turned the code on and replayed the night. At 21:52 the man at 3 Damson Row was held for a code; his number was in his new phone, he typed it, and the barrier opened. At 02:14 phone 2 gave the right password and was held for a code. The code went to Mrs Haverkamp's own phone, abroad: a text telling her a new phone was signing in as her. Nobody typed it, and the barrier stayed shut. The copy still shows 893 exposed, 869 of them with a phone on file; the 24 without one are held for me at the hut until I've seen them in person. So the association also told the 893 to set a new password at their next sign-in, checked against the common list, and Portcullis moved storage to a slow hash with a salt for each password.
options.senior: A password is something you know, and anything known can be copied, guessed or reused. A second factor asks for something you have, here the phone already on file, and only when the risk is new: a phone the app has never seen. It holds even when the password is common, reused and leaked, which is why it beats a stricter password rule. Keep its limits in view: a text-message code can be redirected by someone who takes over the phone number, so an app prompt or a passkey is stronger; changing the phone on file must itself need the old phone or an in-person check; and it never excuses weak storage. Do the storage work too, and force a one-time change for the exposed accounts.

options.text: Store passwords with a slow hash and a salt, so a stolen backup is far harder to use.
options.verdict: Right for the copy, not for her
options.part2: Wojtek moved every password to Argon2id with its own salt, the cost set as high as the barrier's sign-in can bear, each one as its resident next signs in. In the sim I switched the storage to slow and salted, as if the August copy had been stored that way. The count fell from 893 exposed to 353, and 887 accounts would hold. But 353 is exactly the 312 on the common list and the 41 from another website's leak: storage can't hide a password someone can try first or already has. Mrs Haverkamp's is both. At 02:14 phone 2 gave her password and the barrier opened, the same as last night. And the real August copy is still out there, stored the old way.
options.senior: Slow, salted storage is the right way to keep passwords, and NIST and OWASP both ask for it: a salt unique to each password makes each account separate work, and a slow hash with a cost setting makes every check costly. It limits the damage of the next leaked copy. It does nothing for a copy already taken, and nothing for a password that is common or reused. Do it, then force new passwords on the exposed accounts, check new ones against a list of known-bad passwords, and ask for a second proof when a new phone signs in.

options.text: Delete the old backup from the file share and email every resident to say it is gone.
options.part2: The share's owner landed at 18:00, Portcullis deleted the file at 18:10, and Mr Nkemdirim's email reached every resident at 18:30: the file is gone. In the sim I deleted the backup and replayed the night. Nothing moved: 893 of 1,240 accounts exposed, and phone 2 opened the barrier at 02:14. Deleting the share's copy stops the next stranger from finding it, but the 02:14 opening shows that a copy, or Mrs Haverkamp's password from that other leak, was already in someone's hands. Three residents replied to the email to say they were glad it was over.
options.senior: Taking a leaked file down is necessary, and it changes nothing for copies already taken. Assume anything that was public was copied. The response is to make the leaked passwords useless: force new passwords for every exposed account, store them slow and salted from now on, and ask for a second proof when a new phone signs in. The email should tell residents what to do, such as changing the same password on any other site, not that the danger is over.

sim.title: Replay the Quillhaven night, 21:00 to 06:00
sim.lede: You're Mihnea at 21:00 on 14 October, before the night's first gate request. The copy from 3 August holds 1,240 accounts. The adviser's figures are given data: 312 on a password from the common list, 41 more on one from another website's leak, and, stored fast with no salt, 540 more of the rest to treat as exposed. 34 accounts have no phone number on file: 9 of the 312, 1 of the 41 and 14 of the 540. Two new phones ask tonight: at 21:52 the man at 3 Damson Row with his own new phone, at 02:14 phone 2 with Mrs Haverkamp's password. Choose the storage, how many residents use a common password (other choices keep the adviser's 41 and 540 as given), a code to the resident's own phone when a new phone first signs in (an account with no phone on file is held for the guard), a change forced every 90 days, and deleting the backup from the share. The lab counts accounts and gate outcomes only.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to 06:00 as found: 893 of 1,240 exposed, and both new phones open the barrier. Switch to slow and salted: 353 exposed, 887 hold, and 02:14 still opens. Pick 62 on a common password: 103 exposed, never fewer than the common and reused ones. Turn on the code: 21:52 opens after his code, 02:14 stays shut, and the code reaches Mrs Haverkamp's phone. Then try the 90-day rule and deleting the backup: no count moves and 02:14 still opens.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke. At 02:14 a stranger signed in on a new phone with Mrs Haverkamp's real password, which was common, reused on another website, and stored in a leaked backup with a fast hash and no salt. Better storage shrinks how many passwords a stolen copy gives away, from 893 to 353 here, but no storage protects a password someone already knows. Ask for a second proof, a code to the resident's own phone, whenever a new phone first signs in.

steps.title: Authentication: the barrier asked for one kind of proof.
steps.text: Authentication is proving who someone is. Proofs come in kinds, called factors: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone already on file), something you are (a fingerprint). Quillhaven's app asked for one factor, a password, once per phone, then kept a session so that phone stayed signed in. Anyone who knew the password and had any phone could start a new session. That is all phone 2 needed at 02:14.

steps.title: How the app checked a password, step by step.
steps.text: At sign-up, the app ran the password through a hash and stored the jumble, never the password. At sign-in, it hashed what was typed and compared the two jumbles; a match opened a session. What went wrong is in the recipe. A fast hash makes each check cheap, so whoever holds a copy can check guesses cheaply too. With no salt, the same password always gives the same jumble, so one guess checks all 1,240 accounts at once, and a ready-made table of jumbles for common passwords works on every copy. Then the copy itself left the building, on a public file share.

steps.title: Slow and salted: what it buys, and where it stops.
steps.text: Done well, it works in three steps. First, pick a few random letters, the salt, unique to this password. Second, run the password and salt through a slow hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt, with a cost setting as high as sign-in can bear. Third, store the salt, the cost and the jumble together. Now every guess is costly and every account is separate work. The adviser's count falls from 893 to 353. It never falls below the 312 common and 41 reused passwords, because those can be tried first or are known already. Moving existing passwords takes care: each can move when its resident next types it, which leaves anyone who never signs in on the old jumble.

steps.title: Reuse, and why a 90-day rule doesn't help.
steps.text: Mrs Haverkamp's password was common and sat in another website's leak, so it was known before the August copy existed. Trying passwords from one site's leak on other sites is called credential stuffing; it works because people reuse passwords. A forced change every 90 days doesn't stop it: her password was 85 days old at 02:14, and people under a schedule usually make a small change to the old one. NIST SP 800-63B says not to require periodic changes, to force a change when there is evidence of compromise, and to check every new password against a blocklist of common and leaked ones.

steps.title: A second proof from something you have.
steps.text: Multi-factor authentication asks for a second, different kind of proof. Here it runs in steps. A phone the app has never seen signs in with the right password. The app holds the barrier and texts a code to the phone number on file. The barrier opens only when that code is typed into the app. At 21:52 the man at 3 Damson Row typed his code and went in. At 02:14 the code went to Mrs Haverkamp's own phone, abroad, and nobody typed it. What can go wrong: an account with no phone on file (24 of the 893) has nowhere to send the code, so it is held for the guard; and the phone number on file must not be changeable with the password alone.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next night. A new phone sends a password to the gate app. The app compares it with the password store, kept with Argon2id and a salt for each password. A known phone goes straight to the barrier. If the phone is new, the app sends a code to the resident's own phone on file, and the barrier opens only if the code is typed.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next night. Passwords are kept slow and salted, so the next stolen copy gives away 353, not 893. A phone the app knows opens the barrier as before; a new phone waits for a code sent to the resident's own phone on file. At 02:14 that code went to Mrs Haverkamp, abroad, and the barrier stayed shut.

fix.title: The fix: a second proof for new phones, slow salted storage, and new passwords for the exposed
fix.text: When a phone the app has never seen signs in, hold the barrier and send a code to the resident's phone on file; open only when it is typed. Hold any account with no phone on file for the guard to see in person, and let nobody change the phone on file with the password alone. Then force a one-time change for the 893 exposed accounts, checking every new password against a list of common and leaked ones. Store passwords with Argon2id and a salt unique to each, the cost as high as sign-in can bear. Take the file off the share, and tell residents to change the same password anywhere else they used it. Drop any plan for 90-day changes. In the sim, the code turns 02:14 from opened to held, and the code reaches Mrs Haverkamp's phone.

limits: A text-message code is the weakest kind of second factor: someone who takes over a phone number can receive it. An app prompt or a passkey, a sign-in key kept on the phone itself, is stronger.

The second proof is only as strong as the way the phone on file gets changed. If the password alone can change it, phone 2 could have put its own number there first. A lost phone needs a slower, checked path.
It guards the gate, not the copy. The August backup still gives away 893 passwords, which residents may use elsewhere, until each is changed.

explain.seniorTake: Authentication should never rest on one secret a person chose. Passwords leak in three ways, and the defences differ. A stolen copy of your store is answered by storage: a salt unique to each password and a slow hash with a cost setting, so each account is separate, costly work; this decides how many fall. A common password is answered by checking every new one against a blocklist. A reused password, known from someone else's leak, can't be answered by anything you do to storage, so the answer is a second factor: something the person has, asked for when the risk is new, such as a device you have never seen. Forced periodic changes answer none of the three, which is why NIST dropped them. When a copy leaks, assume it was taken: force new passwords on the exposed accounts, take the file down, and say plainly what residents should do. Do storage, blocklist and second factor together; each covers a hole the others leave.

realWorld.title: LinkedIn, June 2012: hashed, then hashed and salted
realWorld.text: LinkedIn's own statement of 12 June 2012 describes "the theft of approximately 6.5 million passwords". It says it had been moving from "a password database system that hashed passwords, i.e. provided one layer of encoding" "to a system that both hashes and salts the passwords", and that "all member passwords now are not only hashed, but also salted". The statement does not name the hash it used.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-63B rev 4: salted, hashed, and costly
realWorld.text: Section 3.1.1.2 says: "Passwords SHALL be salted and hashed using a suitable password hashing scheme." and "The chosen cost factor SHOULD be as high as practical without negatively impacting verifier performance."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-63B rev 4: no periodic changes, but change on compromise
realWorld.text: "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically." "However, verifiers SHALL force a change if there is evidence that the authenticator has been compromised." The 893 exposed accounts are that evidence.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-63B rev 4: check against a blocklist
realWorld.text: When a password is set or changed, verifiers SHALL compare it "against a blocklist that contains known commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords." That check would have caught the 312 common passwords as they were chosen.

realWorld.title: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet: which slow hash
realWorld.text: Its opening list says "Use Argon2id", then scrypt if Argon2id is not available, and "For legacy systems using bcrypt". For bcrypt: "The work factor should be as large as verification server performance will allow".

realWorld.title: OWASP: why the salt, and why not a fast hash
realWorld.text: "A unique salt must be added to each password to prevent attackers from using precomputed lookup tables like rainbow tables." And: "Fast hashing algorithms such as SHA-256 are not suitable for password storage".

asked: How should a system store passwords?
What does a salt protect against?
Why is a second factor stronger than a stricter password rule?
interview.answer: Never store the password, store a hash of it, and use a hash built for passwords: Argon2id first, as OWASP recommends, or bcrypt on older systems, with the cost set as high as sign-in can bear, as NIST SP 800-63B says. Give every password its own random salt and store it beside the hash. The salt means the same password gives different jumbles for different users, so one guess no longer checks every account at once and ready-made tables of jumbles are useless; with a slow hash, each account becomes separate, costly work for whoever steals a copy. When you inherit fast or unsalted hashes, move each password as its owner next signs in, and wrap the old hashes in the slow one at once so dormant accounts aren't left behind. Check every new password against a blocklist of common and leaked passwords, and don't force periodic changes; force a change only when there is evidence of compromise. Storage only decides how many passwords a stolen copy gives away. It can't protect a password that is common or already known from another site's leak, and people reuse passwords. That is why a second factor beats a stricter password rule: it asks for something the person has, such as a phone already registered, so a known password alone is not enough. Ask for it when the risk is new, like a device you have never seen, and prefer an app prompt or a passkey to a text code. A story I'd tell: a gated estate's app stored passwords fast and unsalted, a backup leaked, and a resident's common, reused password opened the barrier at 02:14 from a new phone. Slow, salted storage would have cut the exposed accounts from 893 to 353, and still let that one through; a code to her own phone would have held it.

terms.def: The gated estate in this story: 410 houses behind one barrier, with a guard's hut beside it. Residents open the barrier from a phone app.
The arm across Quillhaven's entrance road. The app opens it; the guard's screen lists every opening with the house number.
The phone app Quillhaven's residents use to open the barrier. Built and run by Portcullis.
The fictional firm that built Quillhaven's gate app and keeps its database.
The group of residents who run Quillhaven's shared affairs. Its chair is Mr Nkemdirim.
The list of every barrier request: date and time, house, which phone asked, and what the barrier did.
Proving who someone is before letting them in. A password, a code from your phone and a fingerprint are all proofs.
A kind of proof: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone on file), or something you are (a fingerprint).
The first time a phone gives the password for an account. After it, the app keeps a session and that phone stays signed in.
A hash that is quick to work out. Fine for checking files, wrong for passwords: whoever holds a copy can check guessed passwords cheaply.
A few random letters added to a password before hashing, different for each password and stored beside the hash. The same password then gives different jumbles.
A hash built for passwords that makes every check costly on purpose, with a cost setting that can be raised. Argon2id and bcrypt are slow hashes.
The number that decides how much work a slow hash does for each check. Set it as high as sign-in can bear, and raise it over the years. Also called a cost factor or work factor.
A slow password hash, the first choice in OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet.
An older slow password hash with a work factor. OWASP lists it for older systems where Argon2id is not available.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project: a volunteer project that publishes free security guidance, such as its Password Storage Cheat Sheet.
The app's organised store of records. Quillhaven's holds every resident's account and password hash.
A saved copy of a database. Portcullis saved one on 3 August, with every password hash inside.
A web folder that anyone with its address can open. Quillhaven's backup was left on one.
A published list of the passwords people choose most often. 312 Quillhaven accounts use one from it, Mrs Haverkamp's among them.
Account data from a website that has become public or fallen into strangers' hands. Passwords from leaks are known to whoever has them.
Using the same password on several sites, so one site's leak opens the others. 41 Quillhaven accounts use a password from another site's leak.
Trying passwords from one site's leak on other sites. It works only because people reuse passwords.
An account whose password you should assume a stranger knows. As stored, 893 of Quillhaven's 1,240; slow and salted, 353.
A second, different kind of proof asked for after the password, such as a code sent to a phone already on file.
Asking for proofs of two or more different kinds, such as a password and a code from your own phone. Often shortened to MFA.
Short for multi-factor authentication.
The phone number an account registered. The code for a new phone goes there. 34 Quillhaven accounts have none.
A sign-in key kept on your own device and unlocked with your fingerprint or screen lock. Nothing to type, so nothing to copy or reuse.
A list of passwords not allowed: common, expected or known from leaks. NIST says every new password must be checked against one.
Forcing every user to pick a new password on a schedule, such as every 90 days. NIST says not to require it.
A ready-made table of hashes for many likely passwords. With no salt, one table works on every copy; a unique salt makes it useless. A rainbow table is one kind.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its SP 800-63B covers how passwords and other proofs should be handled.
NIST's guideline on authentication: salted, hashed and costly password storage, a blocklist check, no forced periodic changes.
A long random secret a program sends to prove which customer it acts for. Being random, it can usually be stored with a fast hash.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A controls A.5.17 and A.8.5 cover authentication information and secure authentication.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC6.1 covers logical access security.

atWork: Find out how your systems store passwords, and check it rather than trusting the design document. It is a common pattern to find, during a migration, a login table whose password column holds fast, unsalted hashes left by an old default. Check four things. Which hash and what cost setting: Argon2id or bcrypt, with the cost as high as sign-in can bear? Is there a salt unique to each password? Is every new password checked against a blocklist of common and leaked passwords, and is any forced 90-day change still switched on that you can drop? And does a new device need a second factor, with the phone on file changeable only by a checked path? If you find fast hashes, move each password as its owner next signs in, and wrap the old hashes in the slow one at once so nobody is left behind. Build Night N5 in Nightwatch (teams, roles, API keys and an audit log; it unlocks after this case, What May You Do, The Borrowed Key, Tokens, The Tenant Upstairs and The Watchman's Book) asks you to store API keys hashed and show each one once. Notice the difference: an API key is long and random, so a fast hash is usually enough there; a password is chosen by a person, so it needs slow and salted. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.5.17 (authentication information) and A.8.5 (secure authentication) expect this storage and a second factor where the risk calls for it; if SOC 2, criterion CC6.1 covers logical access security. Build it in now, with a dated record of the hash, the cost and the second-factor rule, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: A gym's members app stores passwords with a quick hash and nothing random added. A developer finds a copy of its user table in a public folder. The manager says: "We'll switch to a stronger hash tonight, so we're safe." What do you tell her, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The copy already taken keeps its old hashes; new storage only protects future copies, so treat its accounts as exposed and make them set new passwords
Store passwords with a slow password hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt, a unique salt per password and a high cost setting
Common and reused passwords fall anyway, so add a second factor and check new passwords against a blocklist

recall.model: Switching tonight protects future copies, not the one already taken: that copy keeps its old quick hashes, so treat its accounts as exposed and force a reset, making members set new passwords. Then store passwords properly: Argon2id, or bcrypt on an older system, with a unique salt per password and the cost factor as high as sign-in can bear. Move existing passwords as members next sign in, and wrap the old hashes in the slow one at once. Even then, common and reused passwords fall, because they can be tried first or are known from other leaks, so check every new password against a blocklist of common and leaked ones and add a second factor, such as a one-time code to the member's own phone when a new device signs in.

recall.prompt: What does a salt unique to each password protect against?
options: Someone turning a stored jumble straight back into the password
One guess checking every account at once, and ready-made tables of jumbles working on every copy
A resident choosing a password from the common list
A stranger who already knows the password from another website's leak
recall.why: With no salt, the same password always gives the same jumble, so one guess checks every account and a ready-made table works everywhere. OWASP: a unique salt prevents precomputed lookup tables like rainbow tables. It does nothing for a common or already-known password.

recall.prompt: What does NIST SP 800-63B rev 4 say about making users change their passwords on a schedule?

Don't require periodic changes; force a change when there is evidence of compromise
Require periodic changes only for administrators
recall.why: "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically. However, verifiers SHALL force a change if there is evidence that the authenticator has been compromised." People on a schedule usually make small, guessable changes.

recall.prompt: At 02:14, phone 2 signed in with Mrs Haverkamp's real password. Which change would have kept the barrier shut?
options: Storing passwords with a slow hash and a salt for each
A forced password change every 90 days
Deleting the backup from the file share
A code to her own phone on file when a new phone signs in
recall.why: Her password was common and in another site's leak, so storage couldn't hide it; it was 85 days old, so a 90-day rule hadn't fired; deleting the file can't recall copies. Only a second factor, something she had, stopped a stranger who knew it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. New phones now need a code from the phone on file, and the barrier has held every stranger since. In November Portcullis moved passwords to Argon2id with a salt for each one, and each password moved the next time its resident signed in. In March Dilnoza checked a fresh internal copy of the database, kept inside Portcullis this time. 629 of the 1,240 accounts are on the new storage. The other 611 are still stored the old way: fast, no salt. Portcullis says they'll move when those residents sign in.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are 611 accounts still on the old storage, and what should Portcullis do now?

keyIdeas.idea: A password only moves when it is typed, and the app keeps phones signed in with a session, so residents who never sign in again stay on the old hash
Wrap the old hashes now: run each stored fast hash through Argon2id with a salt, and check sign-ins through both layers
Or retire the old ones: clear the 611 fast hashes and make those residents set a new password at next sign-in

coldCase.model: The move only happens when a resident types the password, because that's the only time the app sees it. But the app keeps each phone signed in with a session, so a resident whose phone stayed signed in never types it, and 611 accounts never moved. Any copy made today would still give those away. Don't wait: wrap the old hashes now, running each stored fast hash through Argon2id with its own salt, so no account is stored the old way; at sign-in, check the typed password through both layers, and move it to plain Argon2id then. If wrapping isn't possible, retire the old ones: clear the 611 fast hashes and make those residents set a new password at their next sign-in, through the code to their phone on file.
